    Reading tree-ring data with dplPy¶

    This notebook provides a tour through the capababilities of dplpy.readers(), which reads Tucson format .rwl files (and .csv) into a Pandas DataFrame. This dataframe has one column for each measurement series, indexed by year. The full description of readers can be found in the documentation here: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/io/#readers and the User Guide here: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/guide/reading-writing-data/#ring-width-files-with-readers.

    This notebook uses the sample files shipped in ../tests/data/rwl/ and ../tests/data/csv/, so it runs as-is from the notebooks/ folder of the repository.

    First, we'll import dplPy:

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import dplpy as dpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

dpl.__version__
    import dplpy as dpl import matplotlib.pyplot as plt dpl.__version__
    Out[1]:
    '0.8.0'

    In order to be able to use this notebook 'out of the box', set the paths to where the Tucson .rwl and the .csv files live. These files reflect a range of different data, including several with known formating errors used to test the robustness of readers.py.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    # Sample data shipped with the repo, relative to the notebooks/ folder.
RWL = "../tests/data/rwl/"
CSV = "../tests/data/csv/"
    # Sample data shipped with the repo, relative to the notebooks/ folder. RWL = "../tests/data/rwl/" CSV = "../tests/data/csv/"

    The Basics¶

    At its most simple, you can pass a filename (and path) and get back a year-indexed DataFrame with one column per series. We'll call dpl.stats as well, to give us a quick look at the data that is now in our workspace.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    data = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca533.rwl")
dpl.stats(data)
    data = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca533.rwl") dpl.stats(data)
    ca533.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 34 series covering the period from 626 to 1983

    You should see a success message from dpl.readers, indicating the file type, number of series, and the full time span of the data.

    As data is a Pandas DataFrame, we can append a .plot method to it and use plt. methods from Matplotlib to add axes and a title:

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    data.plot(legend=False, figsize=(9, 4))
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("ring width (mm)")
plt.title("ca533 — raw ring-width series")
plt.show()
    data.plot(legend=False, figsize=(9, 4)) plt.xlabel("Year") plt.ylabel("ring width (mm)") plt.title("ca533 — raw ring-width series") plt.show()

    We can see the raw ring widths in units of mm arrayed through time. We can also use append other methods from Pandas. For instance, we can get a quick sample depth plot by first counting the number of non-NaN values in each row using .count, then using .plot again to display these:

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    data.count(axis=1).plot(figsize=(9, 3))
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("number of series")
plt.title("ca533 — sample depth")
plt.show()
    data.count(axis=1).plot(figsize=(9, 3)) plt.xlabel("Year") plt.ylabel("number of series") plt.title("ca533 — sample depth") plt.show()

    Headers are detected automatically and read attributes are recorded¶

    dplPy automatically identifies where the data rows actually start and records how many header lines it skipped onin df.attrs. The .attrs is once again a feature of Pandas (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.attrs.html) that can store attributes for the dataset, so that this information is carried along throughout your script. readers uses .attrs to store anything unusual during the import process as well as metadata:

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    tx = dpl.readers(RWL + "tx042.rwl")
print("header lines skipped:", tx.attrs["dplpy_header_lines_skipped"])
    tx = dpl.readers(RWL + "tx042.rwl") print("header lines skipped:", tx.attrs["dplpy_header_lines_skipped"]) 
    tx042.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 95 series covering the period from 1473 to 1992 (auto-detected 3 header lines)
header lines skipped: 3

    Metadata in the header is identified and saved¶

    The site and sample metadata is parsed as best as possible from the header by dpl.readers and is saved into df.attrs["dplpy_metadata"]. Alternatively we provide dpl.metadata() which allows you to simply extract the metadata into a Python dict structure:

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    meta = dpl.metadata(RWL + "tx042.rwl")
meta
    meta = dpl.metadata(RWL + "tx042.rwl") meta
    Out[7]:
    {'site_id': 'BSC',
 'site_name': 'Big Bend National Park incl. Camp Springs',
 'species_code': 'PSME',
 'species_name': 'Douglas Fir',
 'country_region': 'Texas',
 'elevation_m': 2057,
 'latitude': 29.25,
 'longitude': -103.3,
 'first_year': 1473,
 'last_year': 1992,
 'investigators': 'Brewster  E.Cook  N.Montagu',
 'n_header_lines': 3,
 'header_raw': ['BSC    1 Big Bend National Park incl. Camp Springs           PSME               ',
  'BSC    2 Texas        Douglas Fir       2057M  2915-10318    __    1473 1992    ',
  'BSC    3 Brewster  E.Cook  N.Montagu                                            '],
 'hemisphere_verified': True}

    Values in meta (or any dict) can then be extracted or printed to the screen (or added to a plot) by using square brackets and the name of the field (called the 'key' in Python) in quotation marks:

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    print(meta["site_name"], "|", meta["species_code"], "-", meta["species_name"])
    print(meta["site_name"], "|", meta["species_code"], "-", meta["species_name"])
    Big Bend National Park incl. Camp Springs | PSME - Douglas Fir

    Data-quality warnings and heads-up¶

    readers reads the file but flags spots worth a human's examination. For instance, a short interior gap (a missing year inside a series not indicated by a negative number), or characters past the last data column (indicating a possibly truncated value). Once again, this information is stored in df.attrs:

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    wa = dpl.readers(RWL + "wa082.rwl")
wa.attrs["dplpy_interior_gaps"]
    wa = dpl.readers(RWL + "wa082.rwl") wa.attrs["dplpy_interior_gaps"]
    wa082.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 23 series covering the period from 1698 to 1983 (auto-detected 3 header lines)

    /tmp/ipykernel_28406/2497868340.py:1: UserWarning: 1 gap sentinel(s) (-999) read as NaN in 1 series (the marker dpl.writers and some archives use for an interior gap).
  wa = dpl.readers(RWL + "wa082.rwl")
/tmp/ipykernel_28406/2497868340.py:1: UserWarning: wa082.rwl: 1 short interior gap (a blank year between measured years -- possibly a dropped value) in 1 series:
    712011: 1900
  wa = dpl.readers(RWL + "wa082.rwl")

    Reading directly from the ITRDB¶

    readers allows you to directly read Tucson formatted tree-ring data from a URL, including from the ITRDB. In the example below, a Pinus echinata site from Oklahoma collected by Dave Stahle is fetched from the ITRDB, and readers warns the user that there is a likely formatting error that should be examined:

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    ok = dpl.readers("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/northamerica/usa/ok049.rwl")
    ok = dpl.readers("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/northamerica/usa/ok049.rwl") 
    ok049.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 443 series covering the period from 1744 to 2020 (auto-detected 3 header lines)

    /tmp/ipykernel_28406/650980834.py:1: UserWarning: ok049.rwl: 1 row had characters beyond the last data column (col 72) that were not parsed -- check for a truncated value:
    LIN152A 1839: read '303', ignored '5'  (looks like a split value)
  ok = dpl.readers("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/northamerica/usa/ok049.rwl")
/tmp/ipykernel_28406/650980834.py:1: UserWarning: ok049.rwl: 1 short interior gap (a blank year between measured years -- possibly a dropped value) in 1 series:
    LIN01A: 1939
  ok = dpl.readers("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/northamerica/usa/ok049.rwl")

    A detective story: catching and repairing an oddity¶

    Reading from the ITRDB is also where surprises turn up. Here is a real one. This European larch site from Mattertal, Switzerland (Hartl and colleagues, ITRDB che413) reads cleanly, but it carries a quirk that dpl.check is built to catch. It is important to practice safe ITRDBing!

    dpl.check is the data-quality companion to readers: it screens a collection and returns problems as a table, one row per finding, each with a severity.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    che = dpl.readers("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/europe/che413.rwl")
    che = dpl.readers("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/europe/che413.rwl")
    che413.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 38 series covering the period from 1596 to 2017 (auto-detected 3 header lines)
    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    findings = dpl.check(che)
findings[["series", "check", "severity", "year_from", "year_to", "n", "message"]]
    findings = dpl.check(che) findings[["series", "check", "severity", "year_from", "year_to", "n", "message"]]
    Out[12]:
    series check severity year_from year_to n message
    0 HCZ0106a RWL_REPEATED_VALUE warning 1769.0 1775.0 7.0 0.01 repeated in 7 consecutive rings, 1769-177...
    1 HCZ0117a RWL_REPEATED_VALUE warning 1685.0 1690.0 6.0 0.01 repeated in 6 consecutive rings, 1685-169...
    2 HCZ0101b RWL_SERIES_OUTLIER warning NaN NaN NaN correlates with the collection at r = 0.555 wh...
    3 HCZ0112b RWL_SERIES_OUTLIER warning NaN NaN NaN correlates with the collection at r = 0.518 wh...
    4 HCZ0102a RWL_SHORT_OVERLAP note NaN NaN 46.0 overlaps the rest of the collection by 46 ring...
    5 HCZ0102b RWL_SHORT_OVERLAP note NaN NaN 46.0 overlaps the rest of the collection by 46 ring...
    6 HCZ0104b RWL_SHORT_OVERLAP note NaN NaN 46.0 overlaps the rest of the collection by 46 ring...
    7 HCZ0103b RWL_SHORT_SERIES note NaN NaN 29.0 29 rings, fewer than 30; too short to crossdat...

    Two series carry a run of the same value, 0.01 mm, for several years in a row. A larch ring of 0.01 mm is not a real measurement. It is the smallest nonzero value the file can hold, and here it stands in for something else. Across the whole file the value 0.01 turns up 217 times in 24 series, so this is a convention, not a typo.

    What does it mean? There are two likely readings, and the file does not say which:

    • a not-measured value, a gap in the record, or
    • a locally absent ring written as a tiny number because some detrending programs historically refused a literal 0.

    Let us look at one of the flagged series.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    che["HCZ0106a"].loc[1766:1778] # this is a run of 0.01 between real rings measurements
    che["HCZ0106a"].loc[1766:1778] # this is a run of 0.01 between real rings measurements
    Out[13]:
    Year
1766    0.84
1767    0.87
1768    0.84
1769    0.01
1770    0.01
1771    0.01
1772    0.01
1773    0.01
1774    0.01
1775    0.01
1776    0.88
1777    0.01
1778    0.98
Name: HCZ0106a, dtype: float64

    Real ring widths sit on both sides of this run of inplausible measurements. That is the case fill_internal is built for. First we mark every 0.01 placeholder as not-measured (NaN), which turns each run into an interior gap. Then fill_internal estimates the gap so the series can be used by tools that reject interior gaps, such as detrend and the crossdating checks. In the code below, we use fill="ARSTAN" to call on Ed Cook's spline based infilling method, which uses information from series with non-missing measurements to help estimate the missing values. Other options (inherited from dplR) include Spline,Mean,and Linear. See here for more: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/utilities/#fill_internal

    If instead we judged these to be locally absent rings, the right action would be to set them to 0, which dplPy keeps as real data rather than a gap. The choice is the analyst's. Here we take the not-measured reading.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    # mark the 0.01 placeholder as not-measured, then fill the interior gaps
gaps = che.mask(che == 0.01)
filled_linear = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="Linear") # linear interpolation infilling
filled_arstan = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="ARSTAN") # use Ed Cook's spline-based ARSTAN infilling
    # mark the 0.01 placeholder as not-measured, then fill the interior gaps gaps = che.mask(che == 0.01) filled_linear = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="Linear") # linear interpolation infilling filled_arstan = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="ARSTAN") # use Ed Cook's spline-based ARSTAN infilling

    The placeholder run is gone, replaced by a smooth estimate that follows the neighboring rings. fill also accepts "Mean", "Linear", "ARSTAN", or a fixed number if you prefer a different estimate. A plot shows the repair in context.

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    ax = filled_linear["HCZ0106a"].loc[1699:1820].plot(figsize=(9, 3.5), color="b", label="after linear infilling")
ax = filled_arstan["HCZ0106a"].loc[1699:1820].plot(figsize=(9, 3.5), color="r", label="after ARSTAN infilling")
che["HCZ0106a"].loc[1699:1820].plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=1, label="raw (0.01 placeholders)")
ax.set_xlabel("Year"); ax.set_ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); ax.set_title("HCZ0106a")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
    ax = filled_linear["HCZ0106a"].loc[1699:1820].plot(figsize=(9, 3.5), color="b", label="after linear infilling") ax = filled_arstan["HCZ0106a"].loc[1699:1820].plot(figsize=(9, 3.5), color="r", label="after ARSTAN infilling") che["HCZ0106a"].loc[1699:1820].plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=1, label="raw (0.01 placeholders)") ax.set_xlabel("Year"); ax.set_ylabel("Ring width (mm)"); ax.set_title("HCZ0106a") ax.legend() plt.show()

    Duplicate IDs merged from separate segments¶

    When a series ID appears more than once but do not have overlapping years of data, readers mimics dplR and joins them into a single series and reports the merge to the user. The idea of this default is that duplicate ID series that do not overlap in time are likely to reflect a single sample that needed to be measured in pieces (e.g due to damage, compression wood, etc.). However, if this is not the case, you can change this default behavior by setting join=False:

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    ca = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca667.rwl")
    ca = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca667.rwl") 
    /tmp/ipykernel_28406/460076291.py:1: UserWarning: Series ST850A had a duplicate ID in separate blocks with no overlapping years (joined into one series).
  ca = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca667.rwl")

    ca667.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 310 series covering the period from -2649 to 2005 (auto-detected 3 header lines)
  1 series combined from non-overlapping duplicate IDs (merged segments):
    ST850A: 2 segments spanning -662 to 453

    Setting join=False will result in series with duplicate IDs being imported as separate series and renamed by appending a number to the series ID.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    ca2 = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca667.rwl",join=False)
    ca2 = dpl.readers(RWL + "ca667.rwl",join=False) 
    ca667.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 311 series covering the period from -2649 to 2005 (auto-detected 3 header lines)
  1 duplicate series ID kept as separate series (join=False):
    ST850A: disjoint block kept as ST850A2

    Poorly formated Tucson files fail informatively (the strict=True default)¶

    Rather than take heroic measures to read an .rwl file and potentially silently corrupt the data, in default mode readers fails to read the broken file and exits with a specific and actionable message identifying the questionable series and the year. This default behavior is set by strict=True:

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    for f in ["akfirmc.rwl", "cana326_error.rwl", "min.rwl", "viet001.rwl"]:
    try:
        dpl.readers(RWL + f)
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"{f}:\n  {e}\n")
    for f in ["akfirmc.rwl", "cana326_error.rwl", "min.rwl", "viet001.rwl"]: try: dpl.readers(RWL + f) except ValueError as e: print(f"{f}:\n {e}\n")
    akfirmc.rwl:
  Cannot read file -- overlapping data:
  Series 'FAD23B' overlaps itself at year 1210: the row beginning 1205 has one value too many (only 5 fit before 1210) -- a misplaced value or mistyped start year.


    cana326_error.rwl:
  Cannot read file -- data after the stop marker: series 'NRX14A' at year 1300. A block under an existing series ID appears after that series' stop marker (likely a mislabeled series ID).

min.rwl:
  Cannot read file -- misaligned fixed-width columns (an embedded space or TAB in a field): series 'SeriesA' at year 1 (field '10 30'); series 'SeriesB' at year 1 (field '200 4') (<TAB> marks a tab).


    viet001.rwl:
  Cannot read file -- overlapping data:
  Duplicate series ID 'BDF02A' (two blocks overlap at year 1640) -- rename or remove the duplicate.

    Salvage mode will do everything it can to read as much of the file (strict=False)¶

    For batch processing, setting strict=False tells readers to recover whatever it reasonably can instead of failing. It may drop an unusable series and salvage the rest, it can join or rename duplicate IDs, and it records every decision and action in df.attrs["dplpy_salvage"].

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    kok = dpl.readers(RWL + "kyrg014.rwl", strict=False)
kok.attrs["dplpy_salvage"]
    kok = dpl.readers(RWL + "kyrg014.rwl", strict=False) kok.attrs["dplpy_salvage"]
    kyrg014.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 33 series covering the period from 1551 to 2005 (auto-detected 3 header lines)
  4 series combined from non-overlapping duplicate IDs (merged segments):
    kok2a: 2 segments spanning 1606 to 2004
    kok2b: 3 segments spanning 1552 to 2004
    kok5b: 2 segments spanning 1714 to 1989
    kok12a: 2 segments spanning 1653 to 2004

    /tmp/ipykernel_28406/1554625663.py:1: UserWarning: Salvaged kyrg014.rwl: dropped 1 series (kok3a:precision_shift)
  kok = dpl.readers(RWL + "kyrg014.rwl", strict=False)

    readers handles mixed measurement precision just fine¶

    A single Tucson file can have series measured at different precisions. In this example, all the TMS* cores at 0.001 mm and all the TWM* were measured at 0.01 mm many years earlier. readers automatically scales each correctly:

    In [21]:
    Copied! 
    tms = dpl.readers(RWL + "TMScombined.rwl")
tms.plot(legend=False,figsize=(9, 4))

    Non-ASCII series IDs are handled correctly¶

    Series IDs containing non-ASCII characters are preserved as-is:

    In [22]:

[c for c in ru.columns if any(ord(ch) > 127 for ch in c)][:6]
